In my role as a cognitive-linguistic therapist, I teach people how to find the structure in their ideas so they can communicate effectively. In essence, I show people how to look at their sea of ideas, find groups, label those groups, and then make sure those labeled groups are working together (i.e., the thesis) and reflecting the reason they are organizing their ideas (i.e., the goal). With their ideas organized, people can then see what they're thinking and, if the task requires it, write those ideas down.

Every act of organizing something - from your things (e.g., socks in a sock drawer) and your time (e.g., steps in a project) to your ideas (e.g., a term paper) and your heart (e.g., a love letter) - builds your ability to take individual items, tasks, and thoughts and create a whole that possibly only you could create. That is, there is no one correct way to organize your sock drawer or write a love letter; the organization of it depends on your experiences, your interests, and your vibe.

I worry that knee-jerk outsourcing of organizational activities, writing or otherwise, will rob us of opportunities to casually develop the organizational skills needed to create structures that reflect who we are - ones that are personal, meaningful, and joyful, because we know we created them ourselves.

Starlink has enormous potential and the ability to establish a truly connected world that can transcend individual government's abilities to censor and control information. In a coming century where data is going to be everything.

SpaceX is basically the only player in town in terms of reliable heavy lift spaceflight. SpaceX is to the space launch industry what the US military is to the global defense industry. comments.body: Child caregivers need and deserve services. But we shouldn't take for granted that so many children are raised by people who are ill with serious, chronic diseases. It's the result of a medical system that shuts many people out until manageable diseases have turned into debilitating ones; a food system, work culture, and environment that makes it terribly hard to make "healthy choices" or avoid pollution; and a foster care system that makes it easier to hand a child over to already-ailing grandparents, even great-grandparents, than to offer material support and drug treatment to parents. The bad news is that this situation is the end result of many, many complex social failings. The good news is that every step that leads us closer to universal health care, climate justice, well-funded and functional public schools, and any number of progressive goals will help to alleviate it.

There is no shielding for these children so they can get educated to build an adult life.  They are already having to live an adult life.

“People are being discharged without the resources they need to be able to care for their loved ones,”
Exactly. And that is not allowed - but the unsafeness of the discharge has to be identified and charted and argued 

I try to council people that they do NOT have to assent to an unsafe discharge. The hospital can’t force you to leave. Note that in one case ‘the hospital arranged home PT’. So why not in other cases?

I was privy to see first hand the process of working with a world class architect and a weak board and museum leadership to design a new museum addition. I wasnt a part of the museum just a friend with a degree in arch so they asked me to sit in. 

Pretty exciting. Wont name the architect (talented), but when he revealed his plans - a fine looking building -  I asked if he had other designs as this one didnt provide for an overall plan of how to deal with existing buildings, or collections spaces and access, among other not insignificant issues. 

He said, and I quote, ‘This is the one I think best. Why would I show you others?’

To be fair, I found out he was also given a limited flawed program commission to not consider the entire campus. Just add a building. 

The museum ended up not moving forward with him, but mostly because they were terrified they wouldn’t be able to raise the money. 

At the time I thought they missed a cool opportunity. In retrospect, I think they also dodged a bullet in this case. Both can be true I figure. Mostly a board and development issue: no deep pockets. Still wonder what better leadership and another architect with a better program would have designed.

It is clearly a very poor indicator of the overall health of the economy, especially for those with few or no assets.  Still, for a very long time, the public has been led to believe that the stock market IS a good indicator of the health of the economy, in part because the media, including the NY Times, always emphasize it, with stories, like this one at the top of the news.  This false perception reinforces political and public policy aimed largely at improving the stock market rather than other elements of the economy, ultimately improving the lives of the wealthy but not the less fortunate. I know I’m going to get a lot of backlash for saying this, but here it goes:  leave your small children at home with a babysitter or family member.  A one year old baby will remember nothing about the trip, and even a four year old will only retain fuzzy memories.  

Travel these days is as difficult as ever.  It seems almost like torture both for the parents and the small children to try to attempt a trip such as this one.  I realize that parents want to enjoy every possible special moment with their children, but it’s OK to have a little time apart.  Parents deserve a break from time to time.

I’m sorry the reporter had such a lousy trip.  Wildfire smoke has become a real issue in the world these days.  In the western United States and large swaths of Canada wildfires have become a fact of life.  Especially in the summer months.  It’s obvious that global climate change is at least somewhat responsible.

Lastly- airline travel is not fun anymore.  Navigating crowded airports, dealing with customs and immigration, surly passengers and workers, long lines, etc.  It can be a nightmare.  I still love to travel, but if there was one thing that would have the greatest impact on my decision to travel it’s flying.

If we are lucky, maybe some changes will be positive, but that is highly unlikely. Extra heat in what is a kind of closed system is going to radically alter what we deem to be normal. This will affect vacations. It is hubris to think the wealthy can maintain their beloved vacation spots in the face of something as big as climate change. People can continue to believe it won’t affect them, but every year, we see how it is affecting everyone. Wealth may allow you to filter the air and purify the water in your home, but it won’t solve the environmental mess outside your doorstep. Change (mostly negative) is already here, not just coming in some distant future.

The time of the impact has passed. 

There doesn't appear to be any immediate reports of a flash or a plume, which is not unexpected. Computer simulations considered the rocket stage coming down in a vertical orientation, which would produce the most debris, but the stage could have easily bellyflopped at an angle instead. (The vertical case was the only one simple enough to be computed.)

Observations from telescopes on Earth could take hours or days of analysis to reveal minuscule hints. They could come up empty, too.

The Korean spacecraft Danuri will pass over the site about eight hours after impact (about 10:35 a.m. Eastern time). Even if it successfully captures an image of where the crash occurred, it could take days or weeks to identify it. 

The process is like finding a needle in a haystack, and the only way you can confirm there's a new needle (crater) is by comparing it with an earlier photograph that shows that the surface at that location was previously pristine.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter will pass over the site in six days.

Is it at all possible that the predictions were wrong, and the rocket stage actually missed? 

No, not unless aliens were able to push it out of the way of the moon. 

Like everything flying around in the solar system, the motion of a rocket stage followed Newton's laws of motion with only slight deviations from additional forces like the solar wind. The uncertainty in where the impact would occur was just a few miles.

I almost went to see his film at a free outdoor film festival near a great surf spot the other day. Could have been like the 70's surf film years, which Jack and I just missed (I'm 56). There is no other place where the prosperity of the EU sits immediately side by side with the poverty of north Africa.

Such is Ceuta.

Those with a historical mind will recall that centuries ago it was the Moors who invaded and dominated what we now know as Spain.  Ultimately pushed out, a capstone of the rule of Ferdinand and Isabella, there remains a lingering shared cultural heritage.

A visitor to Spain soon learns that the Flamenco dance form has roots in Morocco.  A visit to Cordoba must include a stop at the once-huge mosque inside of which Catholics installed a church.

Americans, particularly, need only visit the Alhambra to learn not only that it was once a Moorish castle and stronghold -- but one that was re-discovered" and arguably rescued by a visiting Washington Irving.

Incidents like this recent "invasion" of Ceuta by young Morroccans seeking a better life reminds us that today is simply an accumulation of centuries of history.

comments.body:
Why not let Morocco into the EU? Morocco already has extremely close ties to Europe. It also has something the US doesn't and Spain does: a high speed rail network that would tie directly into the Spanish network through a Gibraltar Tunnel that is already in the works.

The problem isn't migrants. The problem is that Moroccan labor can't get to Europe legally. If Morocco was in the EU, Moroccan nurses, construction workers, and farm laborers could cross into Spain to work and then return home whenever they wanted. Most migrants don't want to permanently live abroad. They want to earn money so that they can build a house for Mom and Dad back home.

Don't believe me? Remember the Polish plumbers that caused the English to panic to such a degree that they left the EU? Well guess what? That flood of Polish plumbers stopped once the Polish economy became strong enough to support them back home.

The secret to controlling migration has always been easy. You let the country sending migrants inside the club. Then a generation of workers make money in Europe doing menial jobs Europeans don't do. They send money home. They return home in thirty years when they retire because by then their home country is prosperous.

People will say Africa isn't Europe, but is that true? The Roman concept of Mare Nostrum is instructive. Maybe the best solution to a host of global problems is to redefine Southern Europe as Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and Turkey.

Gosh, Finland has a population smaller than the state of Massachusetts!  The United States has 57 times more people than Finland. That makes reaching a national consensus here likely to be 57 times more difficult than it is there.

And schools?  Our model of only teaching children is based on the old assumption that schools give you everything needed to prepare for life as an adult. This is absurd in a world now changing as rapidly as it is. By the time you get a passing grade at something in the classroom, half of it is already obsolete.

Finally, let’s look at the truly big picture. We have come to depend on hugely complex supply chains for almost everything by now, including food, consumer goods, and information. As a result we cannot see or evaluate what’s being done to make and deliver all that to us. This is a giant overreach, but it has evolved for centuries by now, so most of us haven’t really noticed.

Now AI is positioned to destroy our reliance on information from unseen sources. We are now being forced to work with each other face to face, locally, where trust is not perfect, but deep fakes are a lot less likely.  We must transition to local sources for food and goods as much as possible. This way, we can see first hand how things are grown, processed, and made. We are being forced to reduce our reliance on giant government and business institutions as they have become unmanageable and often corrupt. This is everyone’s curriculum now, not just for children.

While I admire Mr Pepe's drive to succeed against all odds's , I'm having a hard time deciphering Eric Asimov's terminology.  A glossary would help greatly.

The whites are described as "beautifully textured and saline". Is salinity ("saltiness") a desirable quality in wines? (A little salt makes lemonade more refreshing on a hot day, but a pricey wine isn't typically consumed as a thirst-quencher.)

The 4-year wines are described as "tight and austere, their nuances locked behind a wall of tannins." 
1. I'm unsure what "tightness"  refers to in a wine (though in a  person, it refers to drunkenness). Similarly. "austerity" in a wine, referring to high acidity and tannin content, is usually not considered a good thing, anymore than in an economy. 
2. "Wall of tannins" would, in a much cheaper wine, indicate undrinkability due to excessive astringency, and the need for more aging . While tannins - natural antioxidants and antimicrobials, present in both grape seeds and oak barrels- contribute desirable flavor, they need sufficient time to do so: aging polymerizes and oxidizes the tannin molecules, mellowing their taste by reducing bitterness and astringency.
 (In a "Rumpole of the Bailey" short story, "Rumpole and the Wine Tasting", a wine critic describes a cheap and particularly vile, super-astringent brand of wine by saying that "Serving it would be considered infanticide".)

comments.name: jk
comments.body:
Strict rules around ABA therapy simply won’t work. The needs of these clients are idiosyncratic and shift rapidly as skills change, kids mature, their experiences change, and so on. But the ABA method itself is self- correcting: the practitioner collects data throughout each session; the results are analyzed (note the 2nd “A” in ABA), and the program is regularly adjusted toward reaching the defined goals of the specific program for the specific child. It’s the funding system of insurance payments creating the problems. 

ABA isn’t a “racket”. It is labor-intensive, and until the last decade, there weren’t enough practitioners. Why? Only wealthy families, or parents who could drain their retirement accounts, or mortgage their homes could pay for it. Only when health insurers were required to provide ABA did the case numbers explode. Case in point: Washington State health insurers were required to cover ABA in 2012, and the first ABA service provider arrived in  Olympia. 

For ABA to be worth its cost, it has to be individualized in form and content, carefully monitored by qualified staff, and frequently adjusted, stopped, restarted, increased and decreased, as the data collected in sessions dictate.

For many kids, ABA is THE only effective treatment that will mitigate the disabling aspects of the condition.  ABA therapy is self-correcting. More rules and scrutiny by inexpert regulators will make ABA ineffective, wasteful, and harm the people with autism who need the help.

The other 90% or so have structural issues ranging from concerning to hazardous to perilous. Finding those problems can be time-consuming and messy as they are typically behind walls, above ceilings or are otherwise encased. Further, it often involves assembling original plans and all subsequent renovation plans and may involve lab testing of materials like concrete, reinforcing steel and structural steel to be certain contractors used the type intended by the designers. It then involves a lot of calculations before the remediation process begins. Finding 180 buildings in a row without hazardous structural issues is impossible, unless you are not looking.

The risk is that this shift concentrates their customer base in a small number of large buyers, which can weaken pricing power if those customers have significant bargaining leverage. It can also make revenue less stable because a few major contracts or purchasing decisions may have an outsized effect on overall sales. For investors, this kind of dependence can raise expectations for rapid AI-driven growth while also increasing concern about volatility if demand from those customers slows or shifts. How about today's 20 and 30 year old's stop listening to "influencers" telling them how to live and actually go out there and figure it out. That's what we did.
